qs.q: A 45-year-old woman with chronic plaque psoriasis develops asymmetric arthritis affecting her distal interphalangeal joints and sausage-like swelling of her digits. Which radiographic finding is characteristic of advanced psoriatic arthritis?
o: Pencil‑in‑cup appearance resulting from marked marginal bone erosion.
Widespread periarticular osteopenia while joint spaces remain intact.
Symmetric joint space narrowing accompanied by large subchondral cysts.
Bridging syndesmophytes linking adjacent lumbar vertebrae.
Calcification within hyaline cartilage (chondrocalcinosis) of the knee.
qs.e: Psoriatic arthritis features distinct radiographic changes including the classic 'pencil-in-cup' deformity from bone lysis.

qs.q: A dermatologist evaluates a patient with scaly erythematous patches that closely resemble new-onset psoriasis. Given the clinical guidance for superficial skin lesions, what crucial step must be taken before confirming a psoriasis diagnosis?
o: Exclude a superficial Candida or dermatophyte fungal infection via appropriate tests
Check serum levels of C1 esterase inhibitor to rule out hereditary angioedema
Perform a Giemsa stain to rule out superficial dermal mast cell degranulation
Administer systemic corticosteroids to test for a delayed-type hypersensitivity response
qs.e: Superficial Candida infections can mimic psoriasis, so fungal infections must always be excluded before establishing a new diagnosis of psoriasis. Giemsa stains are used for mast cells rather than diagnosing fungal mimics.

qs.q: A patient presents with severe pruritus and psoriasis-like skin plaques. Years later they develop lymph node and bone marrow involvement. What is the diagnosis?
qs.e: Mycosis fungoides is a chronic cutaneous T-cell lymphoma starting with pruritus and skin plaques, eventually spreading to deeper organs. Treatment is phototherapy.

exam: A 28‑year‑old with sudden pustular eruption on palms and soles after malaria treatment — what is the next diagnostic step and why? — Look for drug‑induced pustular psoriasis; stop the offending drug and obtain a skin biopsy if diagnosis is unclear.
Explain how you would stage this patient’s disease using BSA when a PASI calculator is unavailable. — Estimate % of body surface involved; >10 % indicates severe disease requiring systemic therapy.

A patient with plaque psoriasis presents with new knee pain and nail pitting. What condition should you suspect and what initial investigation is appropriate? — Suspect psoriatic arthritis; obtain plain radiographs of the affected joints.
Why are systemic corticosteroids avoided in chronic plaque psoriasis? — They can precipitate severe rebound flares and pustular eruptions on withdrawal.

In a clinic without phototherapy, which two topical agents provide the best balance of efficacy and safety for moderate disease? — Potent corticosteroid plus a vitamin D analogue; they act synergistically and limit steroid‑related side‑effects.

Describe the Koebner phenomenon and its relevance to patient counseling. — New psoriatic plaques develop at sites of skin trauma; advise gentle skin care and avoidance of unnecessary cuts or scratches.

A patient with severe psoriasis needs systemic therapy but has abnormal liver enzymes; what alternative drug is preferred and why? — Cyclosporine, because it is hepatically safe but requires renal monitoring.

List three cardiovascular risk factors that should be screened in all psoriasis patients and the rationale. — Hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia; chronic inflammation increases atherosclerotic risk.
ai.title: Psoriasis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Psoriasis is a chronic immune‑mediated skin disease with characteristic silvery‑scale plaques. Diagnosis relies on clinical pattern and histology; severity is staged with the PASI or BSA scores. Management combines topical therapy, phototherapy and systemic agents, tailored to resources.

b: Typical distribution: extensor surfaces, scalp, sacrum, elbows, knees
Nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) suggest psoriatic arthritis
sections.p: Psoriasis is a T‑cell driven inflammatory disorder of the epidermis producing well‑demarcated erythematous plaques with silvery scale. Diagnosis is clinical; a skin biopsy shows parakeratosis, neutrophilic Munro microabscesses and elongated rete ridges.

t.b: Confirms pattern and extent; distinguishes from eczema, tinea, or seborrheic dermatitis
Shows parakeratosis and Munro microabscesses; not needed in classic cases

b: Mild: BSA ≤3 %
Moderate: BSA 3–10 % or PASI 3–10
Severe: BSA >10 % or PASI >10
sections.p: Severity guides therapy. The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) >10 or Body Surface Area (BSA) >10 % defines moderate‑to‑severe disease. In low‑resource settings, BSA estimation is often used.

b: Genetic: HLA‑C*06:02, IL23R variants
Immune: Th17/IL‑23 axis activation
Triggers: streptococcal throat infection, HIV, malaria, TB, herbal remedies, trauma (Koebner phenomenon), stress
sections.p: Psoriasis is multifactorial: genetic predisposition, immune dysregulation and triggers. In East Africa, infections and drugs are common precipitants.

b: Plaques on elbows/knees, scalp, sacrum
Guttate lesions in children after sore throat
Pustular eruptions on palms/soles
sections.p: Patients report itchy, sharply demarcated plaques with silvery scale. Variants include guttate (post‑streptococcal), pustular (often precipitated by infection or drugs), and erythrodermic (life‑threatening). Nail pitting, onycholysis and dactylitis raise suspicion for psoriatic arthritis.
Investigations confirm diagnosis, assess severity and screen for comorbidities.

t.b: Needed before systemic agents; if unavailable, use topical therapy only
Triggers severe disease and influences drug choice; if unavailable, treat as severe psoriasis with caution
Screens for latent TB before biologics; if not possible, avoid biologics

t.a: Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI) calculation
t.b: Quantifies severity; guides escalation of therapy

b: Erythroderma: widespread erythema, fever, hemodynamic instability
Severe pustular flare: high fever, leukocytosis
Psoriatic arthritis leading to joint destruction
Cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome
sections.p: Complications can be systemic and life‑threatening.

b: Topicals for mild disease: potent corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues (calcipotriol), coal tar, salicylic acid
Phototherapy (narrow‑band UVB) if UV unit exists
Systemic agents for moderate‑severe disease: methotrexate, cyclosporine, acitretin (avoid in pregnancy)
Biologics (TNF‑α inhibitors, IL‑17/IL‑23 blockers) only where biologic monitoring is feasible
sections.p: Treat the trigger, control skin inflammation and monitor comorbidities. Choose therapy based on severity and resource availability.

b: Re‑assess PASI/BSA every 3 months
Screen for hypertension, diabetes, dyslipidaemia annually
Educate on trigger avoidance (stress, skin trauma, infections)
sections.p: Regular review of disease activity, treatment side‑effects and cardiovascular risk factors is essential.

b: Eczema (flexural distribution, less scale)
Tinea corporis (ring‑shaped, positive KOH)
Seborrheic dermatitis (scalp, greasy scale)
Lichen planus (purple, flat‑topped papules)
Normal CBC does not exclude severe pustular psoriasis
Negative KOH does not rule out tinea if sampling is poor
Mild BSA may underestimate impact if lesions are on visible areas
